area.title: Notification record, persistence and publishing
area.scope: The stored notification behind every page: its fields and validation, status values and reference format, create, save and submit, fulfilment and reference-number reads, hard delete, expiry and the admin guard, what is persisted, the outbox events and GBN-AG payload published on submit, and what reaches PIMS Dynamics. Stops at amend, cancel-amend, copy and soft delete (manage-notifications) and at the list API (notification-list).

sources.role: the owner's decisions: outranks every other source. It sets how the rest are weighed: the prototype wins by default over what the real services do today; only a DR1 judgement on the same difference, or a real constraint the prototype cannot express (persistence, validation, authentication, cross-service behaviour), overrides it.

claims.statement: The ruling's DR1 paragraph has an elision marked [...]: what the omitted words said about the DR1 parity backlog is not recorded.
The ruling does not say what makes a difference 'truly exceptional', so when a question for people is warranted is left open.

The ruling limits DR1 use to clashes between 'the real frontend' and the prototype; it does not say which frontend that is, or whether DR1 judgements apply to differences in the INS frontend, the backends or other repos.
The ruling does not say which override wins when a DR1 judgement and a real constraint the prototype cannot express point different ways on the same difference.
The ruling does not say what a real service does where a real constraint overrides the prototype: whether it keeps today's behaviour or matches the prototype as closely as the constraint allows.
The ruling does not say whether a feature or behaviour a real service has that Design Release 2.1 does not show at all counts as a difference to remove, or is left alone.
The ruling does not say what to do where the code two themes need to touch overlaps, so no boundary keeps their pull requests from conflicting.

claims.statement: Date-only fields such as the arrival date and the exit date accept only a plain calendar date in the form YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-07-21.

claims.statement: A date-only field sent as a date-time, such as 2026-07-21T00:00:00Z or 2026-07-21T00:00:00, is rejected with a 400 rather than having its time part silently dropped.
claims.quote: Jackson's {@code LocalDateDeserializer} is lenient by default: handed {@code 2026-07-21T00:00:00Z} or {@code 2026-07-21T00:00:00} it keeps the date part and drops the rest. A caller that sends a moment where a calendar date belongs would then be told 200, and the day it meant would depend on a zone nobody stated. With leniency off the value fails to parse and the caller gets 400.

claims.statement: The strict-date rule applies to every date-only field, including any added in future, because it is set for the date type rather than field by field; timestamp fields are not affected.
claims.quote: The override is set for the type rather than with {@code @JsonFormat} on each field, so a future {@code LocalDate} field cannot forget it. {@code Instant} binding is untouched.

claims.statement: A timestamp sent where a date-only value is required, or a date-only value where a timestamp is required, is rejected with a 400 Malformed Request rather than a 500.

claims.statement: Storing dates as strings fixed a bug (EUDPA-282) where, under UK summer time, a calendar date was stored as the previous day.
claims.quote: under {@code Europe/London} during BST, {@code 2026-07-21} lands on {@code 2026-07-20T23:00:00Z}, a calendar day early (EUDPA-282).
